item.title: The Daily Star – The unfinished struggle to end the two-finger test in Bangladesh
item.description:
For generations, Bangladesh’s medical and legal systems placed the burden of proving credibility on rape survivors. In 2018, a landmark High Court ruling challenged this culture of suspicion. As the world marks the 16 Days of Activism in 2026 under the theme “Ensure justice, protect survivors, end impunity”, we revisit the struggle to secure the ban on the two-finger test and examine the challenges that remain in translating legal reform into practice.

Imagine a woman who has survived rape. Reporting it was not easy. She had to find the courage to tell others what happened to her body, and then to keep telling it, again and again, to the police, to doctors and to lawyers.

What followed was often another ordeal. A court wanted evidence, so she was sent for a medical examination. This is called a medico-legal examination, and the doctor writes down the findings in a certificate that goes to the court. Later, at the trial, the lawyer for the accused is allowed to question her. This is called cross-examination.

In Bangladesh, for a very long time, both of these steps could involve the same question: was she “habituated to sex”? In plain words, had she had sex before? A doctor might record it in the certificate. A lawyer might ask it aloud in court.

It may sound like a small detail. It is not. A rape case has to answer one question: did she agree to what happened that day? Consent belongs to that moment and to that person’s choice. What she did before says nothing about it. A woman can be married, can have a partner, can earn her living through sex, and still be raped. Yet a finding or a question about her past quietly moves the court’s attention away from what the perpetrator did and towards how the woman has lived. It invites the court to doubt her when it should be asking what was done to her. Neither medical findings about a woman’s sexual history nor questions about her past can establish whether she consented to the sexual act in question. Yet for decades, both practices remained routine in rape investigations and trials in Bangladesh.
Although the two-finger test was banned in 2018, the legal provision that allowed a rape survivor’s character to be questioned in court remained in force until 2022. Photo: AI generated

The challenge to this practice began with a simple but disturbing question. Does this imply that a person who is habituated to sex cannot be a victim of rape? Can a sex worker not be raped? Are sex workers not entitled to justice? Can a married woman not be a victim of intimate partner violence?

A colonial legacy of questioning women

Women in Bangladesh did not encounter this suspicion for the first time in an examination room. It had been written into law and taught in medical manuals. The two-finger test was one expression of a wider pattern in which the burden of proving credibility fell on the woman, while responsibility for violence did not fall on the perpetrator.

The roots of the test in the Indian subcontinent, including present-day Bangladesh, lie in British medical jurisprudence. Manuals such as Norman Chevers’s A Manual of Medical Jurisprudence for India (1870) and later texts by Isador B. Lyon became authoritative references for medico-legal procedures. Historian Hanne Blank reminds us in Virgin: The Untouched History that virginity testing is neither unique to South Asia nor confined to rape trials. It has appeared across cultures and eras. But within the colonial legal-medical framework, it was codified and legitimised here as a tool to question survivors rather than to support them.

The law reinforced it. Section 155(4) of the Evidence Act 1872, rooted in Victorian ideas about sexuality, said that when a person was prosecuted for rape, “it may be shown that the prosecutrix is of generally immoral character”. The underlying assumption was that women might fabricate allegations of rape, so their sexual histories could be used to assess their credibility.

The suspicion has older roots still. In Satirai Kebol Dhorshito Hoy (roughly, “Only the Chaste Are Raped”), her 2015 study for BLAST of how Section 155(4) worked in practice, researcher Fatema Sultana Shubhra points to the Victorian ideas about sexuality that shaped the 1872 law. In that view, a respectable woman was not supposed to feel sexual desire at all, and her duty was to serve her husband. Desire was seen as a male trait or as the mark of women of the lower classes, such as sex workers. A woman who showed it could be treated as unwell.

Shubhra argues that this notion of purity did not disappear with the departure of the colonial rulers. She also notes that the seventeenth-century English judge Matthew Hale described rape as a charge that was easy to make, hard to prove and harder still to defend against, and the rape trial as one in which the complainant herself ends up being tried. According to Shubhra, this view continues to shape the legal culture surrounding rape cases.

The two-finger test became part of this culture of suspicion. By examining the hymen and assessing vaginal laxity, practitioners sought to label women as “habituated to sexual intercourse”. The language pulled attention away from the one question that mattered, consent, and towards the supposed morality of the woman who had come forward.

The questions point to those who faced the heaviest scrutiny: married women, sex workers and anyone whose life did not match what society expected. None of these circumstances can establish consent to a sexual act.

In 2022, Section 155(4) was repealed through an amendment to the Evidence Act. That was an important change, and it came four years after the High Court ban in 2018. But habits within institutions do not disappear just because a provision is deleted.

What the test is and why it fails

A “per vaginum” or two-finger test is an intrusive physical examination in which a doctor inserts two fingers into the vagina of a rape survivor to check whether the hymen is intact and to assess the size of the vaginal opening and vaginal laxity.

None of this proves or disproves rape. Neither the state of the hymen nor vaginal laxity can scientifically establish whether sexual assault occurred or consent was given. Dr Ruchira Tabassum Naved of icddr,b, one of the petitioners, explains that laxity varies from person to person and that the test rests on the faulty notion that a lack of resistance proves consent. But rape often takes place through coercion, intimidation and threats, which can also be implicit, rendering a woman unable to resist. Injuries can typically be found in 70 percent of rape cases, and rape does not involve only the vagina.
The first page of the High Court judgment of April 12, 2018, banning the two-finger test for rape survivors. The court described the practice as “unscientific, inconclusive, and degrading, with no forensic value”.

Advocates describe the practice in three words:

  • Unscientific: it has no forensic value in proving or disproving rape.
  • Traumatic: it is often conducted without consent and has been described as a form of secondary rape.
  • Humiliating: it perpetuates the myth that women lie about rape and places an unfair burden of proof on survivors.

Even as a means of gathering evidence, the examination is questionable, since it usually takes place too late from a medical standpoint. And it places an additional burden on women who already live with the fear of violence from partners and of ridicule and retribution from families and communities.

How the ban was won

Between 2010 and 2014, BLAST (Bangladesh Legal Aid and Services Trust) was part of the SAFE project, a joint effort with four other organisations that aimed to reduce gender-based violence against young women and girls in urban slums. But the advocacy, Akhter says, grew out of BLAST’s everyday work with survivors.

“We began to notice that the cases of sexual violence survivors who sought BLAST’s assistance were either failing to secure any remedy or were becoming entangled in prolonged delays,” she recalls. “We felt compelled to investigate why this was happening.”

Sixty-five cases were selected for in-depth study. Around 2009–10, Fatema Shubhra of Jagannath University reviewed them. Her report, initially unpublished, later became the basis of a book she published in 2015. It pointed to two failures: the medico-legal examination and the degrading cross-examination of survivors in court.

Indian consultant Ashmita Basu, who reviewed more than 50 of the 65 cases, found that the test was being applied indiscriminately to survivors ranging from children to married women. Legal intern Sylvie McCallum Rougerie visited the facilities herself and observed the examinations. She confirmed that they violated the human rights of the women being examined.

In October 2013, BLAST joined a coalition of rights and development organisations and two experts, Dr Ruchira Naved and Dr Mobarak Hossain Khan, to file a writ petition challenging the test. Then came the slow work of persuasion. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare formed committees to draft medico-legal guidelines. Many forensic experts, those involved recall, “could not be persuaded” at first, so the conversations continued and later extended to gynaecologists.

Professor Dr Gulshan Ara of BIRDEM General Hospital told them plainly that the test had no scientific basis. In 2017, five forensic experts stated that it was unscientific and unnecessary.

“The journey from 2013 to 2018 was not easy,” the advocates recall. “Many individuals had to be convinced to appear before the court.”

Key moments

  • 8 October 2013: BLAST, together with Ain O Salish Kendra, Bangladesh Mahila Parishad, BRAC, Manusher Jonno Foundation, Naripokkho, Dr Ruchira Tabassum Naved and Dr Mobarak Hossain Khan, files a writ petition (WP No. 10663/2013) challenging the validity of the test.
  • 10 October 2013: The High Court issues a Rule Nisi and an interim direction to develop comprehensive guidelines for examining and treating survivors of rape and sexual violence.
  • 7 August 2016: The High Court requires forensic experts to give their opinions on the test.
  • 16 August 2017: Experts state that the test is unscientific and unnecessary.
  • April 2018: The High Court bans the test.
  • 21 July 2019: A government circular is issued in light of the directives.

In April 2018, the bench comprising Justice Gobinda Chandra Tagore and Justice AKM Shahidul Huq held that the test was “not scientific, reliable and valid” and violated survivors’ fundamental rights under Articles 27, 28, 31, 35(5), 39(1) and 43(b) of the Constitution. The practice was described as “unscientific, inconclusive, and degrading with no forensic value”. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare chose not to appeal and began implementing a new medico-legal protocol.
Cover of Satirai Kebol Dhorshito Hoy (“Only the Chaste Are Raped”), Fatema Sultana Shubhra’s 2015 study for BLAST, which warned that banning the two-finger test alone might not end institutional victim-blaming.

Eight directives

The decision went beyond prohibiting the test. The court issued eight directives intended to improve the medical and legal response to rape survivors.

The court ordered that the government’s Health Response to Gender-based Violence protocols be made available to forensic experts, doctors, police officers, public prosecutors and other relevant professionals. Doctors and forensic experts were instructed not to use degrading expressions such as “habituated to sexual intercourse” in medical certificates and not to ask about a survivor’s past sexual experiences. Cases requiring deep intravaginal examinations for medical reasons should be referred to gynaecologists.

For children and young girls, per speculum examinations are not mandatory where there is no history of penetration or visible injury. The bimanual test, which is unrelated to the two-finger test and is used for obstetric and gynaecological purposes, should not be performed on rape survivors.

Other directives call for trained doctors and nurses, preferably female physicians, with female police officers or female relatives present during examinations to ensure that the survivor’s privacy is protected. The court also instructed the Nari-o-Shishu Nirjatan Tribunal to prevent lawyers from asking degrading questions that are unnecessary for establishing the facts of the alleged rape.

Taken together, the directives rest on one principle: the medical and legal systems must protect survivors’ dignity rather than subject them to further humiliation.

A ban on paper, a practice in progress

A ruling is not the same as a change in the clinic. In July 2019, a government circular was issued in light of the directives. Yet in April 2023, the Advancing Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights (AdSEARCH) project of icddr,b began a study of how the ban was actually being implemented.

Completed in September 2024, the study covered eight public health facilities and included interviews with lawyers and NGO staff in Dhaka, Dinajpur and Rangpur. The study, along with interviews with those who led the legal fight, identified persistent barriers:

  • Lack of training: awareness of the protocols among police officers, medical professionals and local lawyers remains inadequate.
  • Lack of information: survivors and their families are often unaware of the ban.
  • Legal arrangements: there are no penalties for violating the protocol, which weakens enforcement.

Advocate Kamrun Nahar of Naripokkho says the 2018 ruling “has not yet been effectively disseminated across all the relevant sectors”. She proposes presenting the eight directives in a concise booklet written in plain language and distributing it widely.

Advocate Md. Shahinuzzaman of Ain O Salish Kendra puts the legal position plainly: since the High Court has ruled, compliance is mandatory, and the test cannot be conducted under any circumstances. Nor can a lawyer present its results as evidence of rape in court.

A warning from 2015 now reads like a forecast. Writing three years before the High Court ban, Shubhra cautioned that scrapping the two-finger test alone might not be enough. If Section 155(4) remained in the law, she warned, another medico-legal method could take its place and give the idea of the “immoral” woman a scientific basis, keeping the same suspicion alive through another such test. Her first recommendation was to repeal the clause entirely.

The test was banned in 2018, but the law that allowed a survivor’s character to be put on trial remained in place until 2022. The gap revealed how legal reform can move faster than the institutions and assumptions it seeks to change.
Protesters hold candles and placards demanding justice for rape survivors and an end to victim-blaming. A survivor’s sexual history can never be grounds for dismissing a rape allegation. Photo: Star

The court ended the test in 2018. The clause itself was repealed in 2022. For four years, then, the test was banned while the rule that allowed a survivor’s character to be put on trial was still on the books. That gap is a reminder that a ban is only a beginning. The suspicion underlying the test has to be removed from the law and from the habits of the institutions that apply it.

The steps needed to strengthen implementation are practical and achievable: make information easily available to survivors, display the guidelines in forensic centres, and organise specialised training for doctors, police officers and lawyers.

Beyond the examination room, Dr Naved reminds us that the legal framework still leaves important gaps. Anal, oral and other forms of rape are overlooked in the legislation, and marital rape remains a “huge caveat”.

The two-finger test was imported with a presumption: that a woman accusing a man of rape must first prove she deserves to be believed. The 2018 ruling rejected that presumption in the one place where it was most invasive. Giving effect to that rejection in every clinic, police station and courtroom is the work that remains.

A judgment can prohibit a practice, but only institutions can ensure that it does not return in another form. The responsibility now lies with the health and justice systems to make the court’s directives part of everyday practice.

Prior sexual activity can never be a reason to dismiss a rape allegation. And no survivor should have to endure degrading examinations, questioning or suspicion in the name of an inherited law.

UN Women’s theme for this year’s 16 Days of Activism is “UNiTE to End Violence Against Women and Girls: Ensure justice, protect survivors, end impunity”. The story of the two-finger test is one of a court that delivered justice, directives that promised protection, and a protocol whose implementation still lacks clear mechanisms for accountability.

A.S.M. Riad Arif and Anubhab Chakraborty work at the International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research, Bangladesh (icddr,b).

This article draws on A Collective Effort to Record the Historical Milestones of the Two-Finger Test Ban (AdSEARCH by icddr,b, April 2026).

“Justice without force is impotent, force without justice is tyrannical.” [Blaise Pascal, Thoughts, 1670]

On 19 November, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) delivered its verdict in the case concerning the Application of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide (The Gambia v. Myanmar), commonly known as the Rohingya genocide case. The Gambia, acting informally on behalf of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), had filed the case against Myanmar on 11 November 2019. After seven years of deliberations, the ICJ has concluded that Myanmar has indeed committed genocide against the Rohingya in northern Rakhine State and violated its obligation to prevent and punish genocide. The Hague-based international court has ruled that Naypyidaw must investigate all persons responsible for the genocide and pay compensation to the Rohingya.

The verdict is unique in the sense that the ICJ has, for the first time in its history, directly held a state – Myanmar – responsible for committing genocide, and the Rohingya have accordingly celebrated the ruling. However, while the ICJ has ruled that the perpetrators of the genocide should be punished, it is highly unlikely that the current government of Myanmar will implement the ruling in practice. In fact, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the military-controlled Myanmar government has issued a highly diplomatic response to the verdict, expressing its ‘disappointment’ and pointing out some technical complications in an attempt to undermine the legitimacy of the verdict. On the other hand, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the opposition National Unity Government (NUG) has accepted the ICJ’s judgment and vowed to ensure ‘justice for the Rohingyas’. However, the NUG, which is embroiled in a brutal civil war against the Tatmadaw-controlled government, currently lacks the capacity to implement the ruling.

In fact, only the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) possesses both the legal and material capacity to enforce the ICJ’s verdict. item.title: The Daily Star – Padma Barrage debate: Is Bangladesh repeating India's Farakka mistake?
item.description:
Professor Md Ataur Rahman's article in The Daily Star on 5 November, “Padma Barrage: Why Bangladesh needs it and the challenges ahead”, is the most careful case yet made for the project. It deserves a careful reply. I agree with much of it. A barrage, he writes, cannot create water. Sediment management must be part of how the structure is operated, not a maintenance chore for later. The 9,000-cusec downstream release should be reviewed rather than fixed. The feasibility and engineering reports should be made public. And the project should be run as an integrated river system rather than a standalone structure.

These are the right tests. My argument is that the Padma Barrage, as approved by ECNEC in May, fails them. Measured against Professor Rahman's own conditions, the design risks becoming what its critics fear: a second Farakka, built by Bangladesh on its own river.
The Farakka Barrage in India. Securing a reliable share of the Ganges' dry-season flow is a crucial precondition for the Padma Barrage project. File photo

The first condition already fails

Professor Rahman's first recommendation is to secure an adequate, reliable share of the dry-season Ganges flow. That is the precondition for everything else. Yet the 1996 Ganges Water Sharing Treaty expires on 12 December, less than a month away, and no renewal is in sight.

The pressures run one way. Bihar blames Farakka for siltation and floods and opposes a renewal that maintains the status quo. West Bengal wants more water for its own needs. Under India's federal system, either state can stall New Delhi, as West Bengal did on the Teesta. New Delhi itself is moving away from fixed guarantees, such as the 1977-style clause Dhaka wants, towards shorter terms and availability-based formulae, with Indian demand met first.

Climate change is shrinking the lean-season flow before anyone sits down to share it. The water promised under a guarantee based on historical flows may simply not be there to deliver.

The monsoon is the mirror image. Farakka cannot hold back the Ganges during the monsoon. When Bihar's embankments are threatened, India opens the gates; New Delhi has directed that all 119 remain open. Bangladesh gets a trickle from January to May and a flood from July to September. Our own barrage cannot hold back that flood either. Its gates, too, must remain open from 10 July to 10 October. Its real storage window is when the river recedes from October to December, and after that it can only share out whatever India lets through.

Bangladesh must, therefore, plan for the absence of a guaranteed lean-season flow. A barrage designed on the assumption of one is designed on hope.
Sediment pathways in the Bengal Delta, showing the proposed Padma Barrage, the existing Farakka Barrage and sediment movement through the Ganges–Brahmaputra–Meghna river system. Sediment is essential for sustaining floodplains and building coastal land. Map: Ahad Chowdhury.

The arithmetic of a second Farakka

The project is defended as a means of storing monsoon water for winter. The numbers do not support that description.

The pond holds about 2,900 million cubic metres. Released evenly from January to May, that volume would provide roughly 224 cubic metres per second, or about 7,900 cusecs. The 1996 treaty guaranteed Bangladesh 35,000 cusecs in alternating ten-day periods of the lean season. Storage alone cannot replace what Farakka withholds.

Professor Nazrul Islam and Professor Md Khalequzzaman have worked through the project's own figures in Prothom Alo. Maintaining a combined flow of 698 cubic metres per second in the five distributaries and at the Godagari and Bheramara pumping stations would require 209 cubic metres per second from storage, or only 30 per cent. The other 70 per cent would have to come from the Ganges' live dry-season flow of about 1,295 cubic metres per second. The flow at Pangsha would be split roughly 60:40, reducing the flow towards Goalando by about 40 per cent.

That is the meaning of a second Farakka. Farakka diverts the Ganges upstream to feed the Hooghly, leaving Bangladesh short of water. Pangsha would divert what remains into the southwest, leaving the lower Padma, the Arial Khan, the rivers of Barishal and the Meghna estuary short of water. The planned minimum release of about 9,000 cusecs in March and April is about one-eighth of the roughly 70,000 cusecs that flowed past Pangsha before Farakka.

Professor Rahman is right that the 9,000-cusec figure should not be fixed. But it should be determined by the needs of the river below the barrage, not by what is left after the southwest is served.
An aerial view of vast sandbars in the Padma River. The proposed Padma Barrage risks replicating Farakka's adverse downstream effects within Bangladesh itself. Photo: Rashed Shumon

Sediment: A geologist's objection

I welcome Professor Rahman's statement that sediment must be an operating component of the barrage. But the design does not yet show how that will happen.

The 18 under-sluices, set about 1.5 metres below the main gates, protect the structure and its intakes from bedload. They do not move fine sediment out of a long backwater, and they deliver nothing to the floodplains or the coast. Opening every gate from July to October lets the monsoon pulse pass. But storage begins when the gates close as the river recedes from October to December, when the Ganges still carries a heavy suspended load. That is when the pond will silt up. Professor Islam warns of siltation, erosion and flooding along a stretch of some 145 kilometres from Pangsha to Pankha. Bihar, upstream of Farakka, shows what a rising riverbed does to the people who live beside it.

We are told that Farakka already traps much of the Himalayan sediment load, so Pangsha will receive less. That argument cuts the other way. The sediment that escapes Farakka constitutes most of what the lower delta still receives. Trapping part of it again deepens the sediment starvation of a coast that must build land to keep pace with subsidence and rising seas.
A map showing the proposed Padma Barrage at Pangsha and associated river management works. Diverting water towards the southwest could deprive the lower Padma and its distributaries of adequate flows. Map: IWM

The question for the delta is not one of total tonnage. It is whether sediment still reaches the land that needs it: the floodplains, the tidal basins and the coast. I spent the mid-1980s at Louisiana State University and watched the Mississippi delta lose land because engineers controlled the river without heeding its geology. Padma Barrage risks becoming a Louisiana-style cautionary tale. Diverting more water into the Gorai also diverts sediment into a channel that has been silting up for decades. Without permanent works at the offtake, the revived rivers could choke within years.

The sedimentation projections to 2072 cited by Professor Rahman may answer these concerns. No one outside the project can know, because the projections have not been published.

Approved before questions were answered

Professor Rahman calls for the feasibility and engineering reports to be made public. So do the project's critics. The difference is that the critics asked before approval.

On 22 August, Bangladesh Poribesh Andolon (BAPA) held a discussion in Dhaka that put ten questions to the Bangladesh Water Development Board and its consultants. Where is the downstream impact assessment? How reliable are the predictions for sedimentation, flooding and erosion upstream? Could the barrage weaken our position in the Ganges talks? Why is planning based on outdated data? A month later, Professors Islam and Khalequzzaman reported that none of these questions had been answered and that the feasibility study and its annexes had not been released despite the Right to Information Act.

A Tk 34,497 crore project was approved first, only to be explained later. That is the sequence that gave us the Teesta Barrage, which, as Professor Islam has shown, turned a deep, meandering river into a wide, shallow, braided one. We cannot repeat it on the Ganges on a far grander scale.

There is a diplomatic cost as well. Bangladesh's strongest claim in the treaty talks is that it needs the Ganges' lean-season flow. Presenting the barrage as the answer to Farakka, one that requires no discussion with India, hands New Delhi an argument for releasing less water.
Hardinge Bridge in Pabna, a crucial monitoring point for Ganges flows entering Bangladesh. The proposed Padma Barrage must account for uncertain upstream water releases and declining dry-season flows. Photo: Anwar Ali

What Bangladesh should do instead

The southwest's crisis is real, and doing nothing is not an option. But the choice is not between this barrage and nothing.

1. Pause construction, not the debate. Publish the feasibility report, the sedimentation model and its inflow assumptions, and submit them to independent review before Phase I commits the project to the design.

2. Put the treaty first. Negotiate for a guarantee clause and an environmental flow, and become a party to the 1997 UN Watercourses Convention to strengthen Bangladesh's hand, as Professor Islam urges.

3. Model the worst case. Test the barrage against curtailed Indian releases and flows reduced by climate change, not the averages of the past.

4. Design for sediment, not storage. If a barrage is built, its operating rules must prioritise sediment continuity and riverbed levels over stored volume, with effective sediment bypassing.

5. Guarantee the river below Pangsha. Set a binding minimum flow for the lower Padma and the estuary based on their needs.

6. Build what works now. Remove the sluices and cross-dams that block the distributaries' offtakes, then dredge the offtakes. Restore beels and old river loops for off-channel storage. Extend tidal river management in the coastal polders. Move the southwest away from water-hungry Boro rice towards drought- and salt-tolerant crops.

Professor Rahman ends where I would: the project must be managed as an integrated system. A delta is such a system, comprising water and sediment together. The test for any intervention on the Ganges is the one Farakka failed: does sediment still reach the land that needs it? Until it can be demonstrated that the Padma Barrage will allow sediment to do so, it should not be built as designed.

Dr Ahad Chowdhury is a geologist and environmental scientist. He teaches in the Department of Geology, Geography, and Sustainability at Jefferson Community and Technical College in Louisville, Kentucky, USA.

Sediment: A geologist's objection

I welcome Professor Rahman's statement that sediment must be an operating component of the barrage. But the design does not yet show how that will happen.

Bihar, upstream of Farakka, shows what a rising riverbed does to the people who live beside it.

Trapping part of it again deepens the sediment starvation of a coast that must build land to keep pace with subsidence and rising seas.

The question for the delta is not one of total tonnage. It is whether sediment still reaches the land that needs it: the floodplains, the tidal basins and the coast. I spent the mid-1980s at Louisiana State University and watched the Mississippi delta lose land because engineers controlled the river without heeding its geology. Hardinge Bridge in Pabna, a crucial monitoring point for Ganges flows entering Bangladesh. The proposed Padma Barrage must account for uncertain upstream water releases and declining dry-season flows. Photo: Anwar Ali

What Bangladesh should do instead

The southwest's crisis is real, and doing nothing is not an option. But the choice is not between this barrage and nothing.

1. Pause construction, not the debate. Publish the feasibility report, the sedimentation model and its inflow assumptions, and submit them to independent review before Phase I commits the project to the design.

3. Model the worst case. Test the barrage against curtailed Indian releases and flows reduced by climate change, not the averages of the past.

4. Design for sediment, not storage. If a barrage is built, its operating rules must prioritise sediment continuity and riverbed levels over stored volume, with effective sediment bypassing.

5. Guarantee the river below Pangsha. Set a binding minimum flow for the lower Padma and the estuary based on their needs.

6. Build what works now. Remove the sluices and cross-dams that block the distributaries' offtakes, then dredge the offtakes. Restore beels and old river loops for off-channel storage. Extend tidal river management in the coastal polders. Move the southwest away from water-hungry Boro rice towards drought- and salt-tolerant crops.

Professor Rahman ends where I would: the project must be managed as an integrated system. A delta is such a system, comprising water and sediment together. The test for any intervention on the Ganges is the one Farakka failed: does sediment still reach the land that needs it? Until it can be demonstrated that the Padma Barrage will allow sediment to do so, it should not be built as designed.

Dr Ahad Chowdhury is a geologist and environmental scientist. He teaches in the Department of Geology, Geography, and Sustainability at Jefferson Community and Technical College in Louisville, Kentucky, USA.

item.title: The Daily Star – The price of being a good woman: Family, sacrifice and power in Bangladesh
item.description:
Bangladesh has spent decades celebrating women's advancement. Girls' education, women's employment in the garment industry, expanding professional opportunities and greater participation in public life have become important markers of national progress. Yet the 2024 Violence Against Women Survey, conducted by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) with technical support from UNFPA, presents a profoundly uncomfortable picture. Among ever-married women surveyed, 67.6 per cent reported experiencing controlling behaviour by an intimate partner during their lifetime. The same survey found that 75.9 per cent had experienced at least one form of intimate partner violence, using its broader measures of abuse.

These figures reveal a contradiction that Bangladesh's development narrative has not adequately confronted. Women have become increasingly visible as workers, earners and contributors to national prosperity. But greater economic participation has not necessarily brought a corresponding redistribution of authority within families. A woman may contribute substantially to household income while remaining subject to restrictions on her movements, relationships, reproductive decisions or use of her own earnings.

The contradiction is not simply that traditional attitudes have survived economic modernisation. More importantly, patriarchal arrangements can adapt to economic change. They may accommodate women's employment, benefit from their earnings and continue to demand their obedience. The question, therefore, is not whether Bangladeshi women have made progress. They undoubtedly have. It is why progress in women's economic participation can coexist with persistent inequalities in their intimate lives.

As the world marks the 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence, this tension deserves closer examination. Violence does not emerge independently of the social relationships in which people live. Nor can it be understood solely through its most visible manifestations. The distribution of authority within families, the moral expectations attached to womanhood and the material consequences of refusing to fulfil those expectations all shape women's vulnerability to coercion.

How patriarchy adapts to economic change

Bangladesh's transformation since independence has altered the relationship between women, work and family life. The expansion of export-oriented garment manufacturing from the 1980s created employment opportunities for large numbers of women. Improvements in girls' education, changes in fertility, urbanisation, microfinance initiatives and the growth of service-sector employment have also contributed to shifts in women's economic and social positions.

These developments have not followed a single trajectory. Employment has enabled some women to delay marriage, support their families, develop social networks and exercise greater influence over household decisions. Other women have encountered new forms of insecurity, including precarious employment, harassment and the expectation that paid work should not interfere with established domestic obligations.

The historical significance of women's employment lies partly in its challenge to the assumption that men are the household's principal economic providers. Yet challenging that assumption does not automatically dismantle the authority associated with it. A woman's earnings may become essential to maintaining the family's standard of living without granting her equal control over savings, property or major expenditure. Her employment may be celebrated as evidence of family success while decisions about her mobility, friendships or career remain subject to negotiation with husbands and relatives.
Shefali Begum, 35, earns Tk 300 a day ferrying passengers across a canal adjoining the Kirtankhola River in Barishal, carrying her 16-month-old daughter Sohana on her lap. The economy benefits from women's productive labour, while households continue to depend on their unpaid care work. The photograph was taken in Rasulpur, Barishal, on May 11, 2024. Photo: Titu Das

This is where a familiar understanding of empowerment becomes inadequate. Employment can improve bargaining power, but bargaining power depends on more than income. It is shaped by ownership of assets, access to independent resources, support from relatives, social expectations and the availability of alternatives if a relationship becomes intolerable.

Feminist economist Naila Kabeer's work on resources, agency and achievements is particularly useful here. Economic resources can expand the opportunities for women to make choices, but their possession does not establish whether meaningful choices are available or exercised. A woman may earn an income without controlling it. Conversely, another woman may exercise substantial household authority despite not participating in formal paid employment. The distinction matters because development indicators often measure participation more readily than power. A household can become wealthier without becoming more equal.

The moral economy of sacrifice

The unequal distribution of authority is sustained not only through material resources but also through ideas about what makes a woman respectable. The good daughter is expected to accommodate her family's wishes. The good wife preserves marital harmony. The good mother places her children's needs before her own. These expectations are neither unique to Bangladesh nor uniformly experienced by Bangladeshi women. Care, commitment and mutual responsibility are essential to family relationships, and many women find meaning and satisfaction in them. The difficulty arises when these virtues become obligations imposed disproportionately on women, while their capacity to refuse remains limited.

Consider the expectations surrounding paid employment. A woman who contributes financially may still be responsible for cooking, cleaning, childcare, caring for older relatives and managing the emotional demands of family life. Her ability to perform these responsibilities alongside professional work is frequently admired as a sign of exceptional resilience. But admiration can conceal an unequal arrangement. The question is why all this labour must be performed by the same person in the first place.

Feminist scholarship on social reproduction has demonstrated that economies depend on the everyday work of sustaining people and households. Children must be raised, workers fed, illnesses managed and relationships maintained. Much of this labour takes place outside formal markets, and women perform a disproportionate share of it.

In Bangladesh, the expansion of women's paid employment has made this contradiction particularly visible. The economy benefits from women's productive labour, while households continue to depend on their unpaid care work. Where men do not assume a comparable share of domestic responsibilities, women's economic advancement can increase their total workload rather than free up their time. The result is a peculiar model of progress: women are encouraged to become economically productive without necessarily being released from older expectations of self-sacrifice.

These arrangements are not inevitably abusive. Households distribute responsibilities in different ways, and inequalities may be negotiated without intimidation. But unequal obligations can become coercive when a woman's ability to disagree is constrained by threats, financial punishment, humiliation or fear. The distinction between obligation and coercion is essential. Families make demands on all their members. The problem begins when those demands become systematically unequal and one person's refusal carries consequences that others do not face. At that point, the language of family responsibility can become a means of exercising power.
Two women carry baskets of coal on their heads. Women's employment challenges the assumption that men are the household's principal economic providers, but does not automatically dismantle the authority associated with that role. Photo: Rashed Shumon

When authority becomes coercion

The 2024 BBS and UNFPA Violence Against Women Survey is important precisely because it examines forms of abuse that are often overlooked in public discussions. Alongside physical and sexual violence, the survey documents controlling behaviour and economic violence. Its findings indicate that controlling behaviour was the most frequently reported category among ever-married women. The categories overlap and reflect specific survey definitions; they should not be treated as interchangeable with legal findings of abuse. Nevertheless, the pattern raises important questions about how authority is exercised in intimate relationships.

Coercive control is useful as an analytical concept because it directs attention towards patterns of domination rather than isolated incidents. Monitoring someone's movements, restricting contact with relatives, controlling access to money or using intimidation to enforce obedience may, in combination, create conditions in which a person cannot exercise meaningful autonomy. The harm lies not only in individual restrictions but also in their cumulative effect.

A woman who anticipates punishment for disagreeing may begin adjusting her behaviour before any explicit threat is made. She may avoid visiting friends, abandon professional opportunities or surrender control over her earnings because previous attempts at independence have resulted in conflict or retaliation. Yet coercive control must not be confused with every disagreement or unequal arrangement within a marriage. Partners may disagree about spending, childcare or employment without either seeking to dominate the other. What distinguishes coercion is the systematic restriction of another person's freedom through intimidation, deprivation or punishment.

This distinction is particularly important in a society where the language of protection can sometimes legitimise restrictions. A husband may present surveillance as concern for his wife's safety. Relatives may justify restrictions on mobility by invoking family reputation. Financial control may be defended as responsible household management. The question is whether the woman concerned has a genuine opportunity to disagree. Where refusal is possible only at the cost of humiliation, deprivation or violence, the relationship between protection and control becomes difficult to ignore.

Why leaving is not simply a matter of choice

Public discussions of intimate partner violence frequently return to a deceptively simple question: why does a woman remain in an abusive relationship? The question assumes that leaving is primarily an individual decision. It overlooks the social and economic arrangements that determine whether departure is possible.

For a woman without independent housing, savings or secure employment, separation may threaten her immediate survival. For a mother, decisions about leaving may involve childcare, schooling, custody and the fear of losing contact with her children. Women who support ageing parents or other relatives may face additional financial obligations. Even women with substantial earnings can encounter constraints arising from property ownership, family pressure, reputational consequences or threats of retaliation. The capacity to leave is, therefore, unequally distributed.

Class shapes the options available, but not in a straightforward way. A low-income woman may lack the resources necessary to establish an independent household. A professional woman may have the financial means but face pressure to preserve a marriage because separation would threaten her family's social standing. Age, disability, location and kinship arrangements can create further differences. A woman who depends on a carer may face particular obstacles to reporting abuse. Someone living in a remote area may have limited access to legal assistance or safe accommodation.

These variations matter because the language of empowerment often assumes that women can exercise rights simply because those rights formally exist. The national survey also found that a substantial proportion of women experiencing violence had not disclosed their experiences to anyone. According to the BBS and UNFPA findings, approximately 62 per cent of survivors reported not having disclosed their experiences.

The figure does not establish a single explanation for silence. Women may fear retaliation, doubt that reporting will help, worry about their children or regard certain forms of behaviour as normal. Some may have previously sought assistance without receiving effective protection. What it does challenge is the assumption that silence indicates acceptance.

Disclosure itself can carry risks. A woman who reports abuse may be encouraged to reconcile, accused of damaging family honour or blamed for failing to preserve her marriage. The demand for compromise can become particularly troubling when it falls primarily on the person experiencing violence. The moral language surrounding family unity can, therefore, shape not only how abuse is experienced but also whether it can be challenged.
Bangladesh's achievements in women's employment and public participation are significant, but economic modernisation does not inevitably lead to gender equality. Photo: Star

The family is not outside politics

The household is often imagined as a private space governed by affection, obligation and personal relationships. But its organisation also reflects wider economic and political arrangements. Property laws and inheritance practices influence access to assets. Labour markets determine employment opportunities and income security. Public services affect how families distribute care. Housing costs, childcare provision and access to justice shape the consequences of separation.

These institutions do not determine every household relationship, but they establish the conditions within which individuals negotiate power. A woman who has secure housing, an independent income and access to effective legal assistance possesses alternatives that may be unavailable to someone without those resources. Such alternatives do not guarantee freedom from abuse, but they can alter the balance of power.

This is why the response to gender-based violence cannot be confined to criminal punishment. Legal accountability is essential, particularly where violence, intimidation or unlawful deprivation has occurred. But protection also depends on whether women can obtain assistance without becoming economically destitute or socially isolated. Shelters, legal aid, accessible healthcare, psychosocial support, childcare and effective referral systems are not peripheral welfare measures. They influence whether the right to leave an abusive relationship can be exercised in practice.

The same is true of women's access to property and control over their earnings. These issues reveal a limitation in approaches that treat empowerment primarily as an individual achievement. Women may be encouraged to become confident, financially literate and professionally successful while the institutional conditions restricting their choices remain largely unchanged. The emphasis then falls on women's capacity to overcome inequality rather than on the arrangements that reproduce it.

There is a similar problem with celebrating resilience. Resilience can describe extraordinary courage in difficult circumstances. But when it becomes the expected response to unequal responsibilities or abuse, it risks turning endurance into a feminine obligation. A woman should not have to demonstrate exceptional strength to exercise rights that others take for granted.
Age, disability, location and kinship arrangements shape women's access to resources and support. Women living in remote areas may face additional barriers to accessing legal assistance or safe accommodation. Photo:

Rethinking progress during the 16 Days

The 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence offers an opportunity to question not only violence itself but also the assumptions through which society interprets women's advancement. Bangladesh's achievements in girls' education, employment and public participation are real. They have expanded opportunities and altered relationships across generations. It would be historically inaccurate to dismiss these changes or portray Bangladeshi women as uniformly powerless.

Yet progress cannot be assessed solely through women's growing contribution to the economy. We must also examine whether they have greater control over resources, whether domestic responsibilities are shared more equitably, whether disagreement is respected and whether institutional support exists when intimate relationships become coercive.

These questions require attention to men as well as women. More equal family relationships cannot emerge through changes in women's behaviour alone. They also depend on men's participation in care, their willingness to relinquish unilateral authority and the social recognition that masculinity need not be organised around control.

They also require us to recognise the diversity of family life. Some households have developed genuinely reciprocal arrangements, while others continue to reproduce inequalities despite substantial economic change. Understanding this variation is more useful than treating Bangladeshi families as uniformly oppressive or imagining that economic modernisation inevitably produces equality.

The central contradiction remains. Bangladesh's economic transformation has changed what women contribute to their families. It has not always changed what their families believe they are entitled to demand in return.

A woman may now be expected to help finance the household while continuing to shoulder most of its care responsibilities. Her earnings may be welcomed without her independence being equally accepted. Her sacrifices may be praised even when the conditions demanding them remain unquestioned.

These contradictions do not make women's economic advancement meaningless. They demonstrate why economic participation, however important, cannot serve as a sufficient measure of freedom.

The more difficult measure lies in the everyday distribution of authority: who controls resources, who makes decisions, whose refusal is respected and who can leave without losing the means to live.

Until these questions become central to our understanding of progress, Bangladesh may continue to celebrate women's contributions while overlooking the unequal terms on which many are expected to make them.

Lubna Ferdowsi is a multidisciplinary researcher and writer focusing on gender, identity, geopolitics, history, sociocultural issues and public policy.

These contradictions do not make women's economic advancement meaningless. They demonstrate why economic participation, however important, cannot serve as a sufficient measure of freedom.

The more difficult measure lies in the everyday distribution of authority: who controls resources, who makes decisions, whose refusal is respected and who can leave without losing the means to live.

Until these questions become central to our understanding of progress, Bangladesh may continue to celebrate women's contributions while overlooking the unequal terms on which many are expected to make them.

item.title: The Daily Star – India, Pakistan and the changing priorities of US foreign policy
item.description:
A critical look at US-India relations is essential to understand US-Pakistan ties. It might help dispel a long-held public perception in Pakistan that US-India relations have somehow been a function of the ups and downs in US-Pakistan ties. And that in establishing the extraordinary relationship with India in the last couple of decades Washington has finally “chosen” India over Pakistan.

The foreign policy establishment acknowledges the cyclic nature of US-Pakistan relations. But uplifted by the recent fissures in US-India ties, charmed by President Trump’s compliments, infused by an enduring faith in the US-Pakistan alliance, and confident of Pakistan’s coveted geopolitical salience, it remains ever optimistic that Washington would come back, and relations would be rekindled to their “halcyon” days.

Both the public and official views need revision, based as they are on faulty assumptions that consider the two relationships as competitive and comparable. That is why one keeps hearing successive Pakistan leaders asking the US to treat the two countries equally, and arguing at home that Pakistan needs to keep a balance in relations with China and the US. This is an erroneous view.

The problem is Pakistan cannot wean itself away from the pride of having been a preferred ally of the US once upon a time. But this notion refers to a world of the Cold War days in which the US had a single interest in South Asia, which Pakistan was capable and India was unwilling to advance. That South Asia is no more.
US President Donald Trump meets Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Field Marshal Asim Munir at the White House on September 25, 2025. Washington's renewed engagement with Islamabad need not come at India's expense. Photo: The White House

There is a new world out there. Its complexity and disorder present a multiplicity of security and strategic challenges, its globalised economy offers exceptional opportunities, and its uncertainty compels countries to hedge, expand, and diversify their partnerships. In this world, India and Pakistan would both have roles for the US, though relations with Pakistan would be transactional and of limited bandwidth, and with India strategic and broad-based. These are two different relations, and neither derives from the strength or weakness of the other, or is based on “choosing” one over the other.

Coming to US-India ties, beneath the trade dispute and H1-B visa frictions US-India strategic cooperation and economic relations continue to thrive. There is substantial collaboration on defence production, space, AI, and maritime security.

In a recent piece, Sameer Lalwani of the Carnegie Endowment pointed out that trade rose to its highest level of $240 billion last year. And the new 10-year framework for the US-India Major Defence Partnership calls for advanced exercises and closer defence-industrial ties. Major US tech companies pledged nearly $68bn towards AI infrastructure investments in India last year. Micron, a leading semiconductor firm, opened its first assembly and test facility in India early this year. And recently Applied Materials and Lam Research announced investments in India’s semiconductor industry.

Prime Minister Modi bruised President Trump’s ego by not acknowledging his role in the 2025 India-Pakistan ceasefire. But this has not impacted the substance of relations. Trump has not reversed ties; he has simply put a brake on them.
US President Donald Trump meets Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the White House on February 13, 2025. India remains strategically important to the US despite periodic diplomatic and economic tensions. Photo: The White House

As for tariffs, these have indeed caused strains but they are not India-specific; they are being applied across the board as Trump’s economic instrument and geopolitical weapon. The reality is he would not allow countries to become economic competitors and geopolitical rivals with America’s help and at its expense. US Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Christopher Landau said in his speech at the Rai­sina Dialogue early this year that the US would not repeat mistakes made with China with India.

India was so pampered by President Biden and Trump in his first term that it came to have a sense of entitlement. Now it is complaining about losing its extra-special status.

Indians forget Washington’s critical help in many areas. The US, for instance, has long supported Indian indigenous technology development. GE engines have been central to India’s domestic fighter jet industry. India’s first indigenous fighter aircraft Tejas relied on an F-16 testbed, and its development of a fifth-generation fighter relies on US wind tunnels.

From Pakistan’s standpoint, what is im­­p­ortant is that US-India differences have not impinged on India’s importance for Wash­in­­gton in the US-China strategic competition. And it will likely endure. Any occasi­o­nal adjustment in it will not bring dividends for US-Pakistan ties. We need to delink the two relationships in our analysis.

The bottom line: the US will continue to engage both India and Pakistan as there are no alternatives to each relationship. The alternative to India is India, and the alternative to Pakistan remains Pakistan.

This article was first published under the title “The US & India” in Dawn, an ANN partner of The Daily Star on November 23rd, 2026.

Touqir Hussain is a former ambassador and adjunct professor at Georgetown University.

item.title: The Daily Star – Before Plassey: The origins of the East India Company’s land grab in Bengal
item.description:
In late 1698, Charles Eyre, soon to be appointed governor of Fort William in Bengal, persuaded the viceroy, Prince Azim ush Shan, to grant the East India Company a nishan conferring zamindari rights over the three small townships of Sutanuti, Kalkata and Govindpur in exchange for Rs 16,000 and a liberal disbursement of bribes. It was a move later described by Walter Firminger as the most significant and enduring step taken by the Company between 1690 and 1757 (Walter Firminger, Historical Introduction to the Bengal Portion of ‘The Fifth Report’, Cambray, Calcutta, 1917, p. 374). Firminger has to be taken seriously, and so I wish to investigate briefly how the events of 1698 can be situated within the Company’s quest to acquire territory, in the course of which it transformed from a venture concerned principally, but not exclusively, with commerce and trade into a colonising power that came to rule over large parts of the Indian subcontinent (see my Land, Law and Empire: The Origins of British Territorial Power in India, Cambridge University Press, 2025, on which I have drawn here).

The acquisition of land in India has attracted scholarly interest, but for understandable reasons, the events of the eighteenth century have tended to provide the focus. This was a period, after all, when, following Clive’s victory at Palashi in 1757, the Company acquired territory in Bengal and Bihar on a scale that dwarfed its earlier territorial gains. Compared with the enormity of this land grab, the acquisitions of the seventeenth century were minute, and yet I suspected that in the early decades of the Company, the legal, economic and political foundations were laid for the wholesale plunder that was to follow (see Philip Stern, The Company State: Corporate Sovereignty and the Early Modern Foundation of the British Empire in India, Oxford University Press, 2011; and David Veevers, The Origins of the British Empire in Asia, 1600–1750, Cambridge University Press, 2019). 
 
A modern reconstruction shows Sutanuti, Kalikata and Govindpur, the three settlements over which the East India Company acquired zamindari rights in 1698. Map: P. K. Niyogi/Wikimedia Commons.

Indeed, the signs were there from the very start. Hidden amidst the technicalities of the Company's 1600 charter was a clause that empowered it to acquire, retain and dispose of land, not a provision, it has to be said, that we would expect to find in the founding charter of a private, joint-stock company putatively engaged in commerce. The limited power of these seemingly hubristic sentiments, however, was soon exposed by the conditions early factors encountered in India. Not only were they treated with disdain by Mughal authorities, but the futility of the notion that land could be annexed in the face of opposition from an empire with a massive land army soon came to be recognised. Somewhat against the odds, however, the Company was able to lease a commodious house at the great port of Surat, but the factors were only too aware of their vulnerabilities. They could not resist threats to vacate the premises at a moment’s notice, and Mughal officials repeatedly denied them permission to convert the factory into a defensible space by fortifying it.

Frustrated by the intransigence of Mughal authorities and repeated failures to consolidate its position at Surat, the Company turned its attention to the Coromandel Coast on the eastern side of India. Over the ensuing decades, partly through circumstance and partly through political manoeuvring, relatively secure bases were established, most notably in Madras, Bombay and Calcutta, which emerged as the three principal sites of the Raj. Our understanding of this process is, however, fragile. What is clear is that early incursions were secured through negotiations between Company agents and indigenous authorities, the details of which cannot be fully grasped without an intimate knowledge of competing systems of land administration and the laws governing land, as well as an appreciation of regional balances of political power.
The cover of Land, Law and Empire: The Origins of British Territorial Power in India by John Marriott, published by Cambridge University Press in 2025.

Key to this was the relatively small coterie of Company agents who, by forming a branch of subimperialism, effectively conducted affairs in India (see Eric Stokes, The Peasant and the Raj: Studies in Agrarian Society and Peasant Rebellion in Colonial India, Cambridge University Press, 1973). Given that it took six months for a communication from the directors in London to reach India, the agents, legitimately claiming that they knew conditions on the ground best, were able to act autonomously in all spheres of Company endeavour, including the acquisition of land. Under these circumstances, we might have expected some among them to be versed in land law as a precondition for entering into negotiations with indigenous authorities. This, however, was never the case. To the best of my knowledge, no factor was trained in, or indeed possessed even a rudimentary knowledge of, English land law, let alone Mughal or Hindu codes governing the administration of land. The directors were aware of this deficiency and attempted to address it by shipping out small collections of standard legal texts, but it was a futile gesture.

Two urgent questions arise: How did Company agents approach negotiations over land, and to what extent were these conducted within a framework set by English common law? It seems to me that pragmatism, rather than a coherent, unified strategy, held the key to eventual success. In a piece mischievously entitled ‘In Defense of Ignorance’, Lauren Benton surveys recent work on the legal politics of the Atlantic world in the early modern period (Lauren Benton, ‘In Defense of Ignorance: Frameworks for Legal Politics in the Atlantic World’, in Brian Owensby and Richard Ross (eds), Negotiating Legal Intelligibility in British, Iberian and Indigenous America, New York University Press, 2018). In legal negotiations with Native American communities, she argues, there was a clear separation on both sides between intelligibility and understanding. The absence of legal training among colonisers did not compromise their position; indigenous legal codes became intelligible to them as agents came to know them through experience and the application of more familiar legal analogies. Put simply, they developed the skills to read the legal landscape and act strategically, often in a shifting political climate, to reach settlements that furthered their interests. ‘Understanding is overrated,’ Benton concludes, ‘both as a legal capacity and as an object of historical inquiry. Abilities to “read” political-legal constraints and to engage in legal practices with even basic competence, in contrast, brought enormous dividends.’
 
An imagined meeting between Robert Clive and Mir Jafar after the Battle of Palashi in 1757. The Company’s later territorial gains dwarfed the small acquisitions of the preceding century. Painting: Francis Hayman, c. 1760; National Portrait Gallery/Wikimedia Commons.

I see agents acting with the same intelligibility as the Company strove to acquire territory in the seventeenth century. When its interests turned to the Coromandel Coast, the site chosen was an unprepossessing fishing village with few natural advantages. The directors initially disapproved of any notion of establishing a settlement, but the agents recognised the potential of Madras, which, crucially, being located in a region beyond Mughal control, would not be subject to the same intransigence experienced in Surat. Indeed, in what was a febrile political climate punctuated by warring factions, the local nayak, Venkatappa, saw in an alliance with the Company an opportunity to boost trade and strengthen his position against rival kingdoms. The kaul subsequently granted in 1638 contained unprecedented concessions, including the right to build a fort and the authority to govern Madras for two years. Because the nayak did not hold alienable rights over the land, however, the Company viewed the arrangement through the lens of common law as a fief under his suzerainty.

This plot, largely infertile and providing, at best, poor foundations for buildings, measured only four square miles, but it was to become the Company's first permanent settlement in India. The initial kaul was renewed, and little time was lost in building what became Fort St George. The security it offered attracted native artisans seeking refuge from the conflicts. They settled outside the walls in their thousands, and the population soared. By 1680, the population of Madras stood at approximately 300,000. In a remarkable missive to the St George council, Josiah Child, the most rapacious of Company chairmen, declared that the place might well provide the foundation of a permanent English dominion in India.
Fort St George at Madras, depicted in an eighteenth-century print. Founded on the Coromandel Coast in the 1630s, the settlement gave the Company a fortified base beyond Mughal control. Source: detail of a print published by J. Fielding in 1782, in John Marriott’s collection.

The next great centre of empire, Bombay, was acquired and grew under very different circumstances. Since 1534, when Sultan Bahadur signed a treaty conferring rights on the Portuguese, the small island and port had languished through neglect and were generally considered to have few prospects. The beleaguered Company at Surat, however, looked to Bombay as a means of opening up trade along the west coast, but the Portuguese resisted any such move. Then, in one of those remarkable events of historical happenstance, Charles II married the Portuguese Infanta Catharina in 1662. As part of the deal, Alfonso ceded control of Bombay, which became Charles's personal demesne, much to the dismay of the Viceroy of Goa, Antonio de Castro, who declared that the treaty would threaten the Portuguese presence in the region, not least by forcing vital legal issues over ownership onto the agenda. While the terms of the treaty were facilitated by shared legal traditions between the English and Portuguese, the practical realities facing Portuguese landowners who risked losing their estates were much less readily resolved, particularly since many were prepared to organise armed resistance.

Charles regarded Bombay as an expensive liability. Quite apart from the turmoil over landownership, there seemed little prospect of it becoming a major trading centre. He offered to sell the island back to the Portuguese crown, but the asking price was exorbitant. Instead, following lobbying, the Company stepped in to take control. And so it was that in 1668, under the terms of a royal charter, all rights, territories and appurtenances were transferred to the Company in return for an annuity of ten pounds. In language that revealed the extent to which the charter was conceived within English codes of common law dating back to the medieval period, Bombay would remain holden to Charles and his successors ‘as the Manor of East Greenwich, in free and common socage, and not in capite, not by knight’s service’ (John Marriott, Land, Law and Empire: The Origins of British Territorial Power in India, Cambridge University Press, 2025, p. 158). In effect, this form of tenure exempted the Company from traditional obligations associated with landholding, including labour and military service.
Two views of the English fort at Bombay, published by Philip Baldaeus in 1672. The Company took control of Bombay in 1668, amid disputes over land held under Portuguese rule. Source: Philip Baldaeus/Wikimedia Commons.

The Company’s ambitions for Bombay were realised only gradually. Before fortification was completed early in the eighteenth century, the island faced serious problems. The expense of the fort itself, threats from external forces that resulted in its seizure in 1690, land reclamation and even a mutiny that resulted in the capture of the administration for a year all delayed the mission to develop the site as a major trading centre. Against this background emerged a renewed determination to exploit a long-held interest in Bengal. Following a disastrous attempt to capture Chittagong, the chief agent in the region, Job Charnock, sailed up the Ganges in 1690, looking for a suitable permanent site. He chose three small trading villages. At first glance, this pestilential settlement with few trading links was an unlikely option, but situated on the banks of the Ganges, with impenetrable jungle behind it, the site was defensible. Three years later, Charnock died, and so the reputation of this semi-mythical figure as the founder of Calcutta is somewhat misplaced, except that, in retrospect, his initial choice of the site was inspired.

Thus it was that Charles Eyre took over the administration and applied himself to the task of increasing revenue by acquiring land in the immediate vicinity. The three villages soon to become Calcutta were held by a Hindu family as a jaghir, originally granted by Jahangir in recognition of its help in defeating a local maharaja seeking independence. Under Mughal authority, rights to the land, although complicated, would not normally have been transferable to the Company. But events propelled a different course. 
Job Charnock’s tomb and epitaph in Kolkata. Charnock chose the site of the Company’s future Calcutta settlement. Source: Rangan Datta Wiki/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

In 1697, a revolt led by Subha Singh captured Bengal to the west of the Hugli River. The local nawab sought the help of British ships to defeat the rebels, which was agreed to on condition that full tenurial rights over Calcutta be conceded to the Company. These demands were denied; instead, inferior raiyat rights were offered and subsequently accepted, most likely because they included a provision to fortify the new factory. At this point, and with new confidence, Eyre sought to extend his territorial authority. Fully aware that zamindari rights would be resisted by local zamindars, he approached Prince Azim, the Viceroy of Bengal, who acceded to his wishes. Over the ensuing period, Fort William was completed; as in Madras, its protection attracted the settlement of artisans and labourers and attendant increases in revenue, while ever more land came under the control of the Company as zamindar. By 1717, following a concerted campaign of bribery and extortion, the Company received a farman bestowing the right to trade freely in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa and to build a factory on any site of its choosing.

In a process more complicated than I have been able to convey in this short account, the East India Company established during the seventeenth century the necessary but not sufficient conditions for the acquisition of large swathes of India. Given the ignorance among factors of even the rudimentary features of English common law governing land, negotiations were likely pursued through corrupt and coercive means, particularly when advantageous opportunities opened up. The language of common law occasionally appeared in the drafting of agreements, but it was little more than window dressing to convey a spurious authority by lending legal legitimacy to arrangements whose practical foundations lay elsewhere.
 
A coloured engraving of Fort William in Bengal, belonging to the English East India Company. Printed for John Bowles, it is a reissue of the 1754 original by Jan van Ryne. Image: British Library

The Company’s territorial control was confined to small areas around what became the three great presidencies of Madras, Bombay and Calcutta, but the legal, ideological and economic foundations had been laid for the extraordinary land grab of the following centuries. In this respect, land was a vital aspect of Company endeavour. Without land, there was no protection or reliable source of revenue, and ultimately no empire. And yet land also exposed deep fault lines between commerce and conquest, London directors and factors, the Company and rival powers, and between policy and practice. These tensions were not incidental to the Company’s expansion. They were integral to it.

I have been conscious of the multidimensionality of land. If I have tended to focus on the legal and economic dimensions, it is because I lack the detailed knowledge of indigenous traditions of landownership and administration necessary for a detailed investigation of such aspects as identity, belonging and memory. I await with interest to see whether others better versed in indigenous land cultures rise to this challenge.

Professor John Marriott is a visiting fellow at Kellogg College, University of Oxford, and the author of Land, Law and Empire: The Origins of British Territorial Power in India (Cambridge University Press, 2025).

To the best of my knowledge, no factor was trained in, or indeed possessed even a rudimentary knowledge of, English land law, let alone Mughal or Hindu codes governing the administration of land. The directors were aware of this deficiency and attempted to address it by shipping out small collections of standard legal texts, but it was a futile gesture.

Two urgent questions arise: How did Company agents approach negotiations over land, and to what extent were these conducted within a framework set by English common law? It seems to me that pragmatism, rather than a coherent, unified strategy, held the key to eventual success. In a piece mischievously entitled ‘In Defense of Ignorance’, Lauren Benton surveys recent work on the legal politics of the Atlantic world in the early modern period (Lauren Benton, ‘In Defense of Ignorance: Frameworks for Legal Politics in the Atlantic World’, in Brian Owensby and Richard Ross (eds), Negotiating Legal Intelligibility in British, Iberian and Indigenous America, New York University Press, 2018). In legal negotiations with Native American communities, she argues, there was a clear separation on both sides between intelligibility and understanding. The absence of legal training among colonisers did not compromise their position; indigenous legal codes became intelligible to them as agents came to know them through experience and the application of more familiar legal analogies. Put simply, they developed the skills to read the legal landscape and act strategically, often in a shifting political climate, to reach settlements that furthered their interests. ‘Understanding is overrated,’ Benton concludes, ‘both as a legal capacity and as an object of historical inquiry. Abilities to “read” political-legal constraints and to engage in legal practices with even basic competence, in contrast, brought enormous dividends.’
